name: Pronouns & Possessives
moduleIntroduction: Welcome to the Pronouns & Possessives module! This is where you learn to claim what is yours. The biggest challenge for French speakers is the 'His vs. Her' rule. In French, you look at the object (sa voiture). In English, you must look at the OWNER (his car). This module will help you master these differences.
contrastiveExplanation:
Gender Agreement:
English: Possessives agree with the OWNER. (Tom -> His car).
French: Possessives agree with the OBJECT. (La voiture -> Sa voiture).

Object Pronouns:
English: Objects are neutral. A book is 'It', not 'He'.
French: Objects have gender. (Le livre -> Il).

Possessive Pronouns:
English: Mine, Yours, Hers (No noun after).
French: Le mien, Le tien.

commonErrors.wrong: Muna likes her father (talking about Muna/Male).
commonErrors.frenchConnection: French 'son père'. Student sees 'father' isn't feminine, but English looks at Muna (He).

commonErrors.wrong: I bought a bag. He is nice.
commonErrors.correct: I bought a bag. It is nice.

commonErrors.frenchConnection: French 'Le mon livre' (incorrect even in French, but 'Le mien' logic interferes).

items.questionText: Muna is a student. ___ goes to school in Buea.
items.feedback: Correct! Muna is a male name, so we use 'He'.

items.questionText: Ngono is my sister. ___ is very kind.
items.feedback: Correct! Ngono is a female name, so we use 'She'.

items.questionText: Look at the dog! ___ is running fast.
items.feedback: Correct! For animals (unless we know the name/gender), we use 'It'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'Il' (masculine). English uses 'It' for animals/objects.

items.questionText: My parents are in the village. I miss ___.
items.feedback: Correct! After the verb 'miss', we use the object pronoun 'them'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French structure is reversed (They miss to me). English is SVO (I miss them).

items.questionText: This is my book. Please give it to ___.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Me' is the object pronoun for 'I'.
Correct! 'Your' is the possessive adjective before the noun 'phone'.

items.questionText: I dropped my pen. Can you pick ___ up?
items.feedback: Correct! A pen is an object, so we use 'it'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'le' (masculine). English uses 'it' for objects.

items.questionText: We are students. This is ___ classroom.
Where is Paul? I want to talk to ___.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Him' is the object pronoun for 'Paul'.

frenchComparison.englishStructure: I want to talk to him...
frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses indirect object 'lui'. English uses preposition + object 'to him'.

items.questionText: These are my shoes. I bought ___ yesterday.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Shoes' is plural, so we use 'them'.

items.questionText: That is not my bag. Is it ___?
items.feedback: Correct! 'Yours' is the possessive pronoun (le tien).

items.questionText: Muna and I are friends. ___ play football together.

items.feedback: Correct! Sarah is female, so we use 'her'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'son' (masculine) because 'téléphone' is masculine. English matches Sarah (Her).

items.feedback: Correct! Tom is male, so we use 'his'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'sa' (feminine) because 'jambe' is feminine. English matches Tom (His).

items.feedback: Correct! Object pronoun for animal is 'it'.

items.questionText: They live in Douala. ___ house is big.

items.feedback: Correct! Possessive pronoun at the end of sentence.

items.questionText: The boys are playing. Look at ___.

items.feedback: Correct! Muna is male. We use 'his', even though 'mother' is female. (Le possesseur est masculin).

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'sa' (feminine) because 'mère' is feminine. English matches Muna (His).

items.questionText: Ngono helps ___ father in the shop.
items.feedback: Correct! Ngono is female. We use 'her', even though 'father' is male.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'son' (masculine) because 'père' is masculine. English matches Ngono (Her).

items.feedback: Correct! 'Its' is the possessive form. 'It's' means 'It is'.

items.questionText: That car is not ours. It is ___.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Theirs' is the possessive pronoun (Le leur).
Correct! When the subject and object are the same, use reflexive pronouns.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses reflexive verb 'se couper'. English uses reflexive pronoun.

items.questionText: Paul and I did the work by ___.
I saw a bird. ___ wings were blue.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Its' shows possession for an animal/thing.

items.questionText: Find the error: "This is the mine."
items.feedback: Correct! In English, we never use 'the' before possessive pronouns. Say 'This is mine'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses article 'le' before 'mien'. English does not.

items.feedback: Correct! Traditionally 'his or her' is singular. (Note: 'Their' is common in modern English, but 'his or her' is formally precise for singular).

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: Agreement with singular indefinite subject 'Every student'.

items.questionText: Look at the baby. ___ is crying.
items.feedback: Correct! If the gender of a baby is unknown, we often use 'It'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'Il' (masculine). English uses 'It' for babies of unknown gender.

items.questionText: I saw your car. It is older than ___.
items.feedback: Correct! Comparison: Your car vs My car (Mine).

items.questionText: Did you enjoy ___ at the party?
items.feedback: Correct! 'Enjoy yourself' is a reflexive verb phrase.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses reflexive verb 's'amuser'. English uses 'enjoy' + reflexive pronoun.

items.feedback: Correct! A company is a thing (it), so possessive is 'its'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses indirect object 'lui'. English uses preposition + object 'to her'.

items.questionText: One should be careful with ___ money.
items.feedback: Correct! Formal English uses 'one's' to match the subject 'One'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'son' (his). English uses 'one's' in formal contexts.

items.feedback: Correct! This is the Double Genitive structure: 'A friend of mine'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French structure is 'One of my friends'. English uses 'of mine'.

items.feedback: Correct! 'Each other' implies A looked at B, and B looked at A. 'Themselves' means they looked in a mirror.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses reflexive 'se' for both reflexive and reciprocal meanings. English distinguishes 'themselves' vs 'each other'.

items.feedback: Correct! 'It' is the dummy subject for 'appears'.

items.questionText: Find the error: "Me and Paul went out."
items.feedback: Correct! 'Me' is an object pronoun. As a subject, say 'Paul and I'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses emphatic pronoun 'moi'. English requires subject pronoun 'I'.

items.questionText: If anyone calls, tell ___ I am busy.
items.feedback: Correct! We often use 'them' as a gender-neutral singular pronoun for 'anyone'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'lui' (singular). English uses 'them' (singular they) for indefinite gender.

items.feedback: Correct! In formal English, after 'It is', we use the subject pronoun (It is I). 'It's me' is common informally but less 'correct'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses emphatic 'moi'. Formal English uses subject 'I'.

items.questionText: ___ is a lot of traffic today.
items.feedback: Correct! Use 'There' to show existence. 'It' refers to a specific thing.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses 'Il'. English uses 'There' for existence.

items.questionText: Between you and ___, I don't like him.
items.feedback: Correct! 'Between' is a preposition, so it requires the object pronoun 'me'.

items.questionText: My hair needs cutting. I will do it ___.
Neither of the boys did ___ homework.
items.feedback: Correct! Formally, 'Neither' is singular, so we use 'his'. (Though 'their' is common in speech).

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: Double genitive structure is unique to English.
French uses reflexive 'nous'. English uses 'each other'.

items.questionText: Find the error: "Her and me are going to the market."
items.feedback: Correct! Subject pronouns needed: 'She and I'.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses emphatic pronouns. English requires subject pronouns.

items.questionText: ___ is a nice park in the city.

items.feedback: Correct! In English, verbs like 'wash', 'shave', 'dress' are usually NOT reflexive unless specific emphasis is needed.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses reflexive. English usually does not for daily actions.

items.feedback: Correct! 'Their' is the standard gender-neutral possessive for 'Everyone'.
Correct! Informally 'me' is standard. Formally 'I' (as I am). 'Me' is safer in general use.

frenchComparison.whyDifficult: French uses emphatic 'moi'. English uses object 'me' (informal/standard) or subject 'I' (formal).
